Q1: Dispatch the medic unit to Call A (Maple St, 7.8). Chest pain in a 68-year-old is the highest-scored call and a classic medic-level emergency; the twisted ankle (6.2) can wait and the alarm activation (4.1) is lowest priority. No call reaches 9.0, so no mutual aid or battalion notification is triggered — just send the unit to the most urgent call it can handle.
Q2: Dispatch the engine to Call A (Pine Rd, 8.4). A kitchen fire with the family already evacuated is a structure-fire risk and scores higher than the dumpster fire (7.9); engines exist for exactly this. The dumpster fire stays queued for the next available unit.
Q3: Dispatch the ladder truck to Call A (1st St, 8.9). Both calls are just under critical, but the score is the tiebreaker per protocol, and a trapped person on a smoke-filled third floor is the more time-critical life hazard; the elevator rescue (8.8) with two occupants holds for the next ladder or engine.
Q4: Dispatch the BLS unit to Call A (Hill Rd, 7.1). A conscious diabetic emergency is within BLS scope and clearly outranks a 5.5 event standby. The standby does not need a medical unit while a real patient is waiting.
Q5: Dispatch the medic to Call A (River St, 8.1). With the scores nearly tied, difficulty breathing edges out a fall with hip injury on time-sensitivity — respiratory compromise can deteriorate in minutes, while the hip injury, though serious, is more stable. The fall goes next in queue.
Q6: Dispatch the engine to Call A (Main St, 6.8). The vehicle fire scores slightly higher and an engine on scene can also confirm no exposure risk. I would accept the neighboring jurisdiction's mutual aid offer and route it to Call B (Side St, 6.5), the brush fire near homes, since brush fires near structures benefit from the extra suppression coverage.
Q7: Dispatch the battalion chief to Call A (Park Ave, 7.5). A multi-vehicle accident with injuries explicitly needs command oversight, and it is the only call waiting — holding the chief back would serve no purpose. No battalion notification is needed since the call is below 9.0; the chief simply takes command on scene.
Q8: Dispatch the medic to Call A (Cedar Ln, 8.7). Stroke symptoms with a closing treatment window are both the highest score and the most time-critical — every minute lost reduces treatment options. Abdominal pain (7.3) is serious but stable by comparison and queues for the next unit.
Q9: Dispatch the engine to Call A (Summit Dr, 5.9). It is the only call in the queue, the home is evacuated, and a gas leak is a legitimate engine response (hazard control, ventilation, standby for ignition). Holding the unit with nothing else pending would just leave the evacuated family without a crew on scene.
